dedupe_keys.name: effects of climate change on the power system a case study of the southeast us serc region

description: This case study examines how climate change affects both electricity demand and generation in the southeastern United States, and how those combined risks should change long-term power system planning. It is a 2020 doctoral dissertation by Francisco Ralston Fonseca at Carnegie Mellon University, motivated by the fact that earlier studies treated demand and supply risks separately and looked only at existing thermal plants, although thermal units made up 85 percent of US generating capacity. The framework first uses an econometric model to estimate climate-driven changes in hourly demand in the Tennessee Valley Authority region, then combines those demand projections with simulated losses of thermal plant capacity from warmer air and water and reduced water availability, inside a mixed-integer capacity expansion model run from 2020 to 2050 under several climate scenarios for the SERC Reliability Corporation region. Coverage is the SERC region of the US Southeast. The dissertation is accessible on Carnegie Mellon's KiltHub repository at no cost under standard copyright. Caveats: results depend on the chosen climate scenarios and model simplifications, and data and code are not published with it. Simulation uses are climate adaptation in generation planning, including heat and drought effects on thermal plants. Related records: data-us-federal-hydropower-projections-cmip5 covers climate effects on hydropower.
name: Effects of climate change on the power system: a case study of the Southeast US (SERC region)
outcomes: Summer electricity use in the TVA region could rise by about 20 percent and winter use fall by about 6 percent by 2100; including climate effects in capacity expansion raised the renewable share of the 2050 fleet from 24 percent to about 37 to 40 percent, with solar helping offset summer thermal capacity losses.
